summary:
Hwaruruk: Satellite Fire Records, One Common Standard

Hwaruruk is a fire activity calendar web app connecting NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS detections into a comparable time series. It answers: “Is this month’s observed fire activity above usual levels here?”

Suomi NPP VIIRS observations became available in 2012 alongside MODIS. Different detection capabilities produced a 2.1–3.0-fold discontinuity when uncorrected records were joined, potentially resembling increased fire activity.

We aggregate detections into fire grid-days (1 km cell × day), using overlapping observations to calculate regional, monthly conversion ratios to NOAA-20. Harmonization brought the discontinuity ratio to 0.99–1.03 across all six regions, nearly eliminating the discontinuity. Results were validated against official wildfire records. Areas with rare fires or detections use parent-region assessments; estimated months carry quality grades to communicate data limitations.

The app provides monthly records for 1,114 areas in South Korea, California, British Columbia, Greece, Chile, and New South Wales, spanning six countries across five continents. A repeatable workflow supports future satellite transitions and adds regions through boundary data and one configuration line. Paramedics, firefighters, land managers, and scientists can compare 25 years of fire activity consistently and prepare for fire-prone seasons.
details:
What it does Hwaruruk is a web app (https://hwaruruk.unzipp.cloud) that shows satellite fire detections by region and month, so you can compare any month with the same month in earlier years. We cover South Korea, California, British Columbia, New South Wales, Greece and Chile, down to 1,114 districts. You search for a place, or pick a region and a month. The dashboard shows a map of the detections, the month's value against its usual range (where that month normally falls), a year-by-month calendar heatmap going back to 2001, and the months when fire activity usually concentrates. Each district also has a monthly insight page with daily activity, the same month in other years, official fire records and neighboring districts. The calendar can be saved as a PNG and the data as a CSV. Every screen is in Korean and English.

How it works We downloaded the FIRMS archive and near-real-time CSV files for MODIS, VIIRS S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, about 11 million detections. About 7.8 million were left after keeping presumed vegetation fires and removing static heat sources, low-confidence detections and points outside the boundaries.

VIIRS has 375 m pixels and MODIS 1 km, and one fire leaves many more points in VIIRS. So we count fire grid-days, not points. A 0.01° cell (about 1 km) with at least one detection on one local day counts as 1.

To harmonize the sensors we convert them to the NOAA-20 scale in a chain: Terra alone, Terra plus Aqua, S-NPP, NOAA-20. Each link is a monthly factor per region, the ratio of the two sensors' totals over the years both observed (2012 to 2025 for MODIS and S-NPP, 2019 to 2025 for S-NPP and NOAA-20). In months with little data we pull the factor toward the overall ratio. The MODIS to S-NPP factors mostly fall between 1.5 and 4. This gives each region one monthly series in NOAA-20 units starting in 2001. Districts have too few fires for the MODIS conversion to hold, so district values use VIIRS only and start in 2012.

For each area and calendar month we compute the median and a usual range, which is the 15th to 85th percentile of the same month in past years. The app labels the month as very unusual, above usual, usual range or below usual, and gives its rank among the same month in other years. Butte County had 1,162 fire grid-days in November 2018, the month of the Camp Fire, which is 29.8 times its November median for 2012 to 2025. Districts that average fewer than about 11 fire grid-days a year are too sparse to judge alone, so they borrow the judgment of their parent province or state, and the screen says so.

We checked the result in two ways. First, leaving one year out at a time, the annual error of the conversion is 6.4% to 14.9% depending on the region. Second, we compared with official fire records, which do not depend on the satellite. Against them, the raw stitched series jumps at 2012 by 2.67 times in Korea, 2.54 in California, 2.92 in New South Wales and 2.38 in Chile. After harmonization these ratios are 1.04, 1.25, 1.05 and 0.96. British Columbia went from 4.99 to 2.14 and Greece from 1.96 to 0.71. Both are still outside the 0.75 to 1.33 range we accept, so we report them as inconclusive.

Benefits Emergency responders, land managers and scientists can see on one page whether this month is ordinary for a district and which months usually carry most of its fire activity. The calendar shows which years stood out. All values are in one unit, so a month in 2005 and a month in 2025 can be read on the same scale. Each view has its own URL, so it can be shared.

Intended impact MODIS is near the end of its operation. We want the 25-year record to continue on VIIRS without a break, so that the baseline does not have to restart. The same pipeline runs for all six regions with one command.

How it is creative We test the harmonization against official fire statistics as well as between satellites. Counting cell-days removes much of the resolution difference before any factor is applied. We did not want sparse districts left blank, so they show the parent region's judgment and say so.

What we considered We compared grid sizes from 0.1° to 0.01° before choosing 0.01°. For Chile and New South Wales, official records are compared by fire season starting in July. The app says on screen that its values are not a count of fire incidents, not burned area and not a real-time alert, and that small fires are often missed. In Korea, 91% of official fires of 100 ha or more had a NOAA-20 detection in the same district within two days. For fires under 0.1 ha it was 5%.

Tools Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1 MCD14; VIIRS 375 m VNP14IMG, VJ114IMG, VJ214IMG), official records from the Korea Forest Service, CAL FIRE, BC Wildfire Service, NSW NPWS, Hellenic Fire Service and CONAF, boundaries from geoBoundaries and the BC Data Catalogue. Pipeline: Python, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib, Jupyter notebooks generated and run per region by one script. Backend: Java 21, Spring Boot 3.5, Gradle, PostgreSQL, Flyway; four services (catalog, time series, spatial, insight). Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, React Router, TanStack Query, Tailwind CSS 4, MapLibre GL, ECharts, three.js, Vitest. Deployment: Vercel for the frontend, API server behind Cloudflare Tunnel.
